title: Resilience Tactical Sprint — Cheatpad (Annotated Draft)
content:
Purpose:
- Quick-reference annotated deck for SEs and ops during pilot/rescue sprints.
- Focus: keep customer integrations live under token/latency pressure, show predictable economic choices, and preserve UX.

Intended audience:
- Field SEs, Platform Sellers, Customer Reliability Engineers, Onsite solution architects.

High-level flow (slides):
1) One-line framing (30s): why resilience matters for inference customers
   - Customer pain: unpredictable latencies, cost spikes, model drift interruptions.
   - Redwood win: unified fallbacks + observability = predictable customer experience.
   - Speaker notes: open with a single customer anecdote: mid-market fintech saw 40% error spikes during peak morning batch; fallback rules saved the day.

2) Rapid qualify checklist (60s): quick litmus test during first call
   - Are they latency-sensitive (SLA < 500ms)? yes/no
   - Do they have bursty daily traffic? yes/no
   - Are they willing to accept variant model quality for availability? yes/no
   - If Yes to two or more -> resilience play recommended
   - Speaker notes: use this to decide whether to pitch reserved capacity vs hosted with fallbacks.

3) Four resilience levers (main slide)
   - Routing: region/model tier routing (primary -> fallback -> cheap fallback)
   - Caching: prefix + KV reuse for repeated prompts
   - Batching & timeouts: graceful degradation window + early token cutoff
   - Quantization & model variants: switch to 8-bit/quantized variant if throughput saturation
   - Annotated examples: include concrete latency/cost tradeoffs per lever (ballpark numbers)

4) Live incident roleplay (5–7 min)
   - Scenario: customer pilot call; production endpoint returns intermittent 503s at 09:35; API token consumption doubles during morning batch.
   - Roleplay script:
     SE: "We see increased 5xxs and token spend — can you confirm if model batch size changed or front-end replay is happening?"
     Customer Eng: "We pushed a job that replays user logs but not sure why spike"
     SE script steps:
       1) Switch request routing to fallback model (policy: latency-first).
       2) Enable prefix cache for repetitive assistant prompts.
       3) Reduce max_tokens and set early_timeout=250ms for critical routes.
       4) Flip autoscale to conservative burst cap (Dedicated) or throttle on hosted API.
     - Observable checks: model latency heatmap, token-cost spike per minute, rate of 5xxs.
   - Outcome: restore 95th pct latency to SLA, cut token spend 30% within 8 minutes.

5) Quick command crib (for field SEs)
   - Example API patch (pseudo): set routing_policy: [{primary: gpt-rw-large, fallback: gpt-rw-fast, mode: latency}], set cache: {prefix:true, ttl:60s}, set timeout: 250ms
   - Console paths: Console > Routes > Edit > Fallbacks; Console > Metrics > 95th latency -> set alert at +20%

6) Economics cheat (single slide)
   - Show three sample profiles (small app, mid-market, high-throughput): cost delta when switching variants, impact of caching (tokens saved %), throughput improvement with batching
   - Key line to say: "Fallbacks are not free — but targeted use reduces SLA hits and total incident cost (pager fatigue + lost revenue)."

7) Objection handling snippets
   - "We can't accept lower-quality outputs" → answer: "We only route critical, low-context responses to fallback; run A/B on non-critical flows and surface evals."
   - "We want deterministic answers" → "Pin model version + use canary + automated quality regressions — we surface eval alerts to you."
   - "We need proof it will work" → "Offer a short 48h resilience pilot with step-capture: metrics baseline -> simulated load -> mitigate. Use our pilot kit (link in artifacts)."

8) Runbook (triage checklist) — two-minute scan
   - 1) Confirm scope (routes affected, percent of traffic)
   - 2) Check capacity/queue depth on Dedicated GPU pools or region limits on hosted
   - 3) Apply quick mitigations in this order: (a) routing fallback, (b) cache enable, (c) reduce max_tokens, (d) throttle non-essential routes
   - 4) Notify: stakeholders, customer SRE, account lead; open incident in the shared triage board (Linear link template)
   - 5) Postmortem starter: collect prompt set and top 50 failing calls, baseline eval of fallback model quality

9) Short scripts for customer demos (copy/paste ready)
   - "During a simulated load, we'll flip routing to a latency-optimized variant and show you: latency, token cost, and percent of responses using fallback in realtime."
   - Walkthrough: 1) baseline capture, 2) apply load (script link), 3) flip policy, 4) compare metrics

10) Open questions / Risk table (annotated)
   - Risk: fallback produces unacceptable hallucinations on domain-specific prompts. Mitigation: seed a safety layer and only route structured outputs (e.g., summaries) to fallback. Action: Research team to run prompt-evals (linked).
   - Risk: billing surprises when caching mis-configured. Mitigation: preset cache TTL and show token-savings estimate. Action: add ticket for console default.

11) Playbook variants (when to choose what)
   - Hosted + fallbacks (fastest onboarding) -> choose for small pilots and integrations with limited security needs
   - Dedicated with conservative routing -> choose for throughput-critical customers who need isolation
   - Private (VPC) -> choose for regulated customers where private control plane + KMS required

12) Appendix: 1-page cheat cards
   - Rapid commands, Linear/Jira templates, Slack incident blurbs, sample evaluation prompts, checklist PDF link.

Notes to self (meta):
- This is intentionally short — aim for a 6–8 slide demo + 1 pager for ops.
- Add real customer numbers from Q4 pilot (ask Asha for anonymized metrics).
- Validate cost ballparks with Finance (Michael).
- TODO: produce 1-click console play for "route-to-fallback" (engineering backlog: GTM-402).

Appendix: speaker-script excerpts (for rehearsals)
- Opening: "Our job in the first 90s is to convince engineering that a short resilience play will reduce your incident surface and save 2x in incident ops for the pilot window."
- When asked about quality: "We treat fallbacks as a staged downgrade — they apply to non-core flows first. We'll show you evidence before any live rollback."
